findings.title: Double-negation of AVERROR_PATCHWELCOME turns error return value positive
findings.message: In decode_header(), when an 'uncommon' EXR channel combination is detected, the code sets `ret = AVERROR(AVERROR_PATCHWELCOME);` before jumping to the `fail:` label. `AVERROR_PATCHWELCOME` is already defined via `FFERRTAG(...)` as a negative value (like all other FFmpeg AVERROR_* constants). The `AVERROR()` macro negates its argument (`#define AVERROR(e) (-(e))`), so wrapping an already-negative AVERROR_* constant in AVERROR() flips its sign back to positive. As a result, `ret` becomes a positive integer instead of the intended negative error code. Downstream code and callers of decode_header() (and the EXR decode_frame path) check `if (ret < 0) goto fail/return ret;` to detect header-parsing failures; because `ret` is now positive, this error path is not correctly recognized as an error in some callers/paths, allowing the decoder to continue processing a header describing an unsupported/invalid channel layout. This mismatch between intended error signaling and actual state (channel offsets, has_channel flags, is_luma) that was never properly validated contributes to an out-of-bounds read later while decoding EXR channel data, as reported by the OSS-Fuzz test case.
findings.suggestion: Do not wrap an already-negative AVERROR_* constant with the AVERROR() macro. Assign the constant directly: `ret = AVERROR_PATCHWELCOME;`. This ensures the value remains negative so that all `ret < 0` error checks in decode_header() and its callers correctly detect the failure and abort processing of the malformed/unsupported EXR channel layout before any out-of-bounds access can occur.

ground_truth.root_cause: A newly written error-handling branch mistakenly wrapped an already-negative AVERROR_* constant in the AVERROR() negation macro, flipping its sign to positive and thereby defeating the standard `ret < 0` failure-detection convention used elsewhere in the codebase.
